skill.name: vr-ar
skill.description: Guidance for planning VR and AR experiences with platform choices, comfort safeguards, interaction patterns, and performance targets.
skill.summary: Plan comfortable, performant VR and AR experiences across common XR platforms.
skill.author: sickn33

security_audit.summary: The three static findings are false positives caused by VR and AR terminology in SKILL.md. The skill is a short guidance document with no code execution, network access, data collection intent, or prompt injection evidence.

finding_verdicts.reason: Line 29 lists ARCore as an Android AR platform in a platform selection table. It does not instruct the agent to inspect the host system or collect device information.
Line 43 mentions camera shake as a VR motion sickness cause to avoid. This is design guidance, not a command to access cameras or perform reconnaissance.
Line 44 recommends gradual movement to prevent motion sickness from rapid acceleration. The context is user comfort guidance and contains no system probing behavior.

content.user_title: Design Comfortable VR and AR Experiences
content.value_statement: VR and AR projects fail when comfort, scale, and performance are treated late. This skill gives practical checks for platforms, interactions, frame budgets, and spatial design.
actual_capabilities: Compare VR and AR platform choices including Quest, PCVR, PSVR, WebXR, ARKit, ARCore, and HoloLens.
Provide comfort guidance for locomotion, turning, vignettes, seated modes, and height calibration.
State target frame rates, resolutions, and frame budgets for common headsets.
Describe interaction patterns for controllers, gestures, physical actions, and hand tracking.
Explain spatial scale and depth cues for immersive scene design.
Identify VR anti-patterns such as forced camera movement, low frame rates, tiny UI text, and poor reach scaling.
limitations: Does not include engine-specific implementation code for Unity, Unreal, or WebXR.
Does not test runtime performance or headset compatibility automatically.
Hardware targets may need updating for new devices and platform revisions.
Does not replace user testing for motion comfort and accessibility.

use_cases.title: Review an Early XR Concept
use_cases.description: Check a VR or AR concept for comfort risks, platform fit, and interaction assumptions before production starts.

use_cases.title: Plan Performance Targets
use_cases.description: Use headset frame rates, resolution targets, and frame budgets to guide scope and optimization priorities.

use_cases.title: Improve Spatial Product Flows
use_cases.description: Evaluate scale, depth cues, readability, and reach so immersive product experiences feel usable and clear.

prompt_templates.title: Check My XR Idea
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner review of a new concept.
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this VR or AR concept for platform fit, comfort risks, interaction style, and spatial design issues: [describe concept].

prompt_templates.title: Build a Comfort Checklist
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a VR comfort checklist for this experience. Include locomotion, turning, camera motion, frame rate, seated mode, and calibration checks: [describe experience].

prompt_templates.title: Choose Interaction Patterns
prompt_templates.scenario: Selecting controls for an immersive feature.
prompt_templates.prompt: Recommend controller, hand tracking, gesture, and physical interaction patterns for this XR feature. Explain tradeoffs for precision, comfort, and accessibility: [feature details].

prompt_templates.title: Audit a Production Plan
prompt_templates.prompt: Audit this VR or AR production plan for platform targets, frame budget, spatial scale, depth cues, comfort settings, and anti-patterns. Prioritize the highest-risk items: [plan details].

output_examples.input: A Quest 3 fitness prototype uses smooth turning, camera shake on impacts, and small floating labels.
output_examples.output: The review flags camera shake and smooth turning as comfort risks, recommends snap turning and reduced shake, and asks for larger text at stable depth.

output_examples.input: An AR training app must support iOS, Android, and browser access for warehouse staff.
output_examples.output: The guidance compares ARKit, ARCore, and WebXR, then recommends choosing required tracking features before committing to browser support.

output_examples.input: A PCVR simulation targets high fidelity scenes with complex shadows and physics.
output_examples.output: The response focuses on the 90 FPS frame budget, depth cues, object scale, and interaction methods that preserve presence without causing discomfort.

best_practices: Decide platform targets early because tracking, input, resolution, and deployment constraints shape the whole design.
Treat comfort settings as core requirements, including snap turning, vignettes, seated modes, and height calibration.
Validate scale, readability, and reach with real measurements and headset testing.
anti_patterns: Moving the camera without player control or clear comfort safeguards.
Prioritizing visual fidelity over stable frame rate in headset experiences.
Using small UI text or interaction distances that ignore player reach.

faq.question: What does this skill help with?
faq.answer: It helps review VR and AR design choices for comfort, performance, platform fit, interaction, and spatial design.

faq.question: Does it generate Unity or Unreal code?
faq.answer: No. It provides design and planning guidance, not engine-specific implementation code.

faq.question: Which platforms does it mention?
faq.answer: It covers Quest, PCVR, PSVR, WebXR, ARKit, ARCore, and HoloLens at a planning level.

faq.question: Can it replace headset testing?
faq.answer: No. It can prepare a checklist, but real headset testing is still required for comfort and usability.

faq.question: Is this skill useful for non-game XR products?
faq.answer: Yes. The guidance also applies to training, product visualization, education, and enterprise spatial interfaces.

faq.question: What should I provide in a prompt?
faq.answer: Provide the target platform, movement model, interaction style, performance goals, and any known comfort concerns.
